players.product: High-density AI data-center colocation / powered infrastructure (ex-Bitcoin-mining conversion)

quarterly_data.signal: The AMD agreement takes Core Scientific to approximately 1.1 GW of total contracted billable capacity, representing more than $24 billion of base contracted revenue. Two customers have now each committed to over 500 MW across five campuses each: CoreWeave at 590 MW of total contracted capacity (grown from a 16 MW lease at the Auburn campus in 2024) and AMD at 530 MW in its initial agreement. Management frames the market as shifting from evaluating companies on the deals they announce to assessing their ability to execute: 'Value is not announced, it is delivered.'
quarterly_data.figure: ~1.1 GW total contracted billable capacity; >$24 billion base contracted revenue

quarterly_data.signal: GAAP colocation revenue rose to $137 million, a significant sequential increase driven by beginning to bill 437 MW in mid-July. Second quarter cash SG&A was approximately $36 million, a $4 million sequential increase driven primarily by one-time professional fees associated with the recent debt financing. The quarter ended with approximately $1.8 billion of liquidity. CoreWeave contract revenue is recognized on a straight-line basis over the 12-year lease terms, effectively pulling future contractual escalators forward.
quarterly_data.figure: $137 million GAAP colocation revenue; cash SG&A ~$36 million; ~$1.8 billion liquidity

quarterly_data.signal: Ahead of schedule and currently billing for 437 MW of capacity. Billing began on 437 MW in mid-July, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter, after substantially completing four of the five CoreWeave campuses ahead of the end-of-summer target. Management stresses that delivering hundreds of megawatts of high-density infrastructure 'requires far more than access to power' - it requires an integrated development and operating platform - and that the AMD sites are not greenfield: equipment is secured, contractors are on site across the five campuses, and at Pecos the building shell is essentially complete.
quarterly_data.figure: 437 MW billable, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of Q1

quarterly_data.signal: Management expects another meaningful step-up in colocation revenue in the third quarter and views the low $30 million range as a reasonable quarterly cash SG&A baseline; no explicit SG&A or EBITDA target was given. On delivery: Pecos is the lead AMD site and is on track for initial megawatt delivery in the first half of 2027, about half of the 530 MW AMD contract will be delivered in 2027 and the other half in 2028, with Hunt, Auburn, Muskogee and Dalton Phase III progressing through design, procurement and construction and ramping through the end of 2028. Based on current labour and long-lead equipment constraints, the target is roughly 600 MW of delivery in 2028, which management calls a great annual cadence for the business.
quarterly_data.figure: ~600 MW delivery target in 2028; ~half of the 530 MW AMD contract in 2027, half in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: AMD holds an exclusive reservation right to lease as much as two additional gigawatts on top of the initial 530 MW - the path to the announced up-to-2.5 GW partnership. That power would come from a combination of incremental grid-connected power, capacity progressing through load studies, and behind-the-meter solutions across Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee; both Pecos and Muskogee have the potential to support up to 1 GW of leasable capacity. Any reserved capacity would be signed as direct AMD leases on substantially similar terms to the leases signed today, and while the reservation stands Core Scientific will not market that capacity to other customers.
quarterly_data.figure: up to 2 GW additional capacity reserved for AMD (up to 2.5 GW partnership total); Pecos and Muskogee up to 1 GW leasable each

quarterly_data.signal: All-in build cost is expected to range from approximately $11 million to $12 million per megawatt, covering construction labour and on-site execution; owner-furnished equipment (transformers, switchgear, generators, chillers, pumps, liquid cooling systems, power distribution and control systems); and soft costs and general conditions through design, permitting, utility interconnect, energization, commissioning and rent commencement. At that rate the initial 530 MW requires approximately $6 billion of capital, which the company expects to finance through project-level bonds using the same SPV structure already used for CoreWeave. About $2 million per megawatt has already been deployed across the portfolio with just about $1 billion in commitments across these projects, and Core Scientific is prepared to invest up to approximately $1 billion more to advance roughly 500 MW of initial build-outs ahead of customer contracts.
quarterly_data.figure: $11 million-$12 million per megawatt; ~$6 billion capex for the initial 530 MW

quarterly_data.signal: Cost per megawatt has risen versus the CoreWeave sites, where labour and equipment were secured starting in early 2024. Equipment costs are up year over year, partly on tariffs and partly on supply-chain constraints and availability, but 'the thing that's primarily driving the cost of construction today is labour' - large general contractors, electrical subcontractors and mechanical trades are saturated with work and scarce across a number of competitive U.S. geographies. On demand, management says data center capacity is still in very short supply and that large-scale GPU contracts are being signed today whose GPUs 'do not have a home yet', with a lot of GPUs sitting on the ground after late deliveries across the industry, which should tighten data-center supply further.

Power development at Pecos: an analyst noted an ERCOT update due August 7 covering roughly 815 MW, and management confirmed about 300 MW of that is the on-grid load study for Pecos with the rest behind-the-meter; given the uncertainty on the timing of that next 300 MW of on-grid power, the next megawatts at Pecos will be driven by the behind-the-meter strategy. Core Scientific is in advanced conversations with natural gas suppliers, has done preliminary planning on lateral pipeline development to the Pecos and Muskogee sites, and has held integrated conversations with on-site generation equipment providers - evaluating turbines, reciprocating engines, linear generators and fuel cells, with the technology choice varying by site geography, environmental conditions and supply-chain availability. The critical path per site is either the time to build the lateral pipeline or generation equipment manufacturing and production capacity. Capital was released for substation construction earlier this year across multiple sites, other sites are pad-ready for utility energization, and the full shell for the first 185 MW at Pecos will be complete within weeks.
quarterly_data.figure: ~815 MW pending the ERCOT update (~300 MW on-grid load study at Pecos); 185 MW first shell at Pecos

quarterly_data.signal: The Bitcoin-mining-to-AI conversion is nearly complete: Core Scientific ended June with nearly 30% fewer miners online than at the end of the first quarter and is now self-mining at only two sites, running that business primarily to offset contractual power costs during the wind-down, which continues over the remainder of the year so that 2027 starts with a clean sheet of paper. Having spent the past year converting existing power capacity from Bitcoin mining to high-density colocation, the next phase complements that with selective acquisition of powered land and development of new sites: a new site pipeline of more than 2 GW of potential incremental power has been identified, with initial capacity potentially available from late 2028 through 2030, and management hopes to bring a new site to market by year-end. The Hunt County, Texas acquisition earlier this year is representative of that pipeline.
quarterly_data.figure: nearly 30% fewer miners online QoQ, self-mining at two sites; >2 GW new-site pipeline (late 2028-2030)

contracts.signal: Four of the five CoreWeave campuses were substantially completed ahead of the end-of-summer target, taking the program to 437 billable megawatts - nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter - and driving GAAP colocation revenue to $137 million. Dalton Phase II, the fifth and final campus and the last 150 MW of the CoreWeave build-out, begins delivering at the end of 2026 and is on track for full completion in early 2027. The relationship began as a 16 MW lease at the Auburn campus in 2024 and has since expanded to 590 MW of total contracted capacity; revenue is recognized straight-line over the 12-year lease terms, pulling contractual escalators forward. Auburn and Dalton become fully leased once the AMD-credit-supported neocloud leases are added.
contracts.units: 437 MW billable of 590 MW contracted; 150 MW remaining at Dalton Phase II
contracts.value: $137 million GAAP colocation revenue in the quarter

connects_to.relationship: AI data-center colocation capacity leased to AMD - 530 MW across five campuses on 15-year leases (direct triple-net at Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee, plus AMD-credit-supported neocloud leases at Auburn and Dalton)

contracts.signal: Commercial partnership with AMD for up to 2.5 GW of data center capacity. The initial agreement represents more than $14 billion of base contracted revenue across 15-year agreements with 2.5% annual escalators, with Core Scientific delivering 530 MW across five sites: approximately 380 MW directly to AMD under a triple-net lease across Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee, and the remaining approximately 150 MW across Auburn and Dalton supporting an unnamed neocloud under a modified gross lease for which AMD provides full credit support for the full 15-year term. The credit support carries no equity step-in rights, protecting Core Scientific's equity in the projects. Core Scientific issued AMD a warrant struck at current market levels, vesting subject to certain commercial conditions. The platform is an integrated colocation platform engineered to support AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with a close-coupled design framework aligned to AMD's GPU and CPU technology roadmap. Pecos is the lead site with initial megawatt delivery in the first half of 2027; about half the contract delivers in 2027 and half in 2028. The build requires approximately $6 billion of capital at $11 million-$12 million per megawatt, to be financed through project-level bonds. AMD additionally holds an exclusive reservation right on as much as two additional gigawatts at Pecos, Hunt and Muskogee.
contracts.units: 530 MW across five campuses (~380 MW direct triple-net + ~150 MW AMD-credit-supported neocloud lease); up to 2.5 GW including the reservation
contracts.value: more than $14 billion of base contracted revenue over 15 years with 2.5% annual escalators
contracts.type: data-center colocation lease and capacity reservation
